newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Templeton fund sues Hungary retailer Fotex.
newsitem.headline: Templeton fund sues Hungary retailer Fotex.

text.p: Templeton Emerging Markets said on Wednesday it is suing Hungarian retailer Fotex for violating minority shareholders' rights and failing to comply with Hungarian securities regulations.

"This is an example where in emerging markets sometimes the people that control these companies think minority shareholders don't count for anything and they do whatever they want," Mark Mobius, president of Templeton Emerging Markets Fund, told Reuters.
Gabor Varszegi, Fotex's founder and general manager, denied Templeton's accusations and accused the fund, a subsidiary of Franklin Resources Inc, of attempting a hostile takeover.
"This is the first hostile takeover attempt in Hungary," Varszegi told a news conference after Templeton announced two suits had been filed in Hungary.

Mobius said Varszegi, through his Panama-based holding company Blackburn International, had tried to increase his control over Fotex with convertible bond issues that were not open to minority shareholders.

He said Templeton had voted for two of the four bond issues by mistake "because we were misled in the meeting by their translator about the terms and conditions". Two issues of the series totalling $20 million were subsequently cancelled.
Mobius, whose fund owns 10 percent of Fotex, said Varszegi also failed to disclose when Blackburn obtained a 25 percent plus one vote interest in Fotex, Hungary's biggest retailer.

"The basic gist of this is we feel Varszegi...was trying to get a majority control of Fotex through the issuance of a convertible bond which was unavailable to most shareholders," Mobius said in a telephone interview from Romania.
"In other words, the way he structured it made it impossible for small shareholders to take the convertible bond and even large shareholders like ourselves could only get a limited amount.
"So the end result of it was that it would have been to dilute the shares," said Mobius, who is the co-ordinating manager of funds totalling $12 billion.

A statement released by Templeton's Hungarian law firm, Seward & Kissel, said the convertible bonds were designed so that after four issues Varszegi would be able to convert and obtain a shareholding of more than 50 percent in Fotex.

"This control would have happened sooner if minority shareholders had not made a stand against Blackburn International at the last General Meeting in May 1997 to reject the proposal to immediately convert and to cancel the next two remaining issues," the statement said.

Varszegi said the statement regarding the purpose of the bond issue was "simply a lie" and accused Templeton of attempting to take over the retailer, whose shares have slumped from 565 forints in 1994 to under 100 forints last year.
"I suppose that Templeton's people can read a balance sheet and they realise that Fotex is grossly undervalued," he said.
Varszegi said the conditions of the bond issue had been published in advance of a November meeting where they were approved, and that no-one had been misled.
He added that there was no requirement in Hungarian law for Blackburn to disclose when it had obtained a 25 percent plus one stake.
"Blackburn is a Panama-registered limited company and this point of corporate law does not apply," he said.
On the Budapest Stock Exchange, Fotex shares closed at 139 forints, down three.
In 1996, the diversified retailer which sells everything from electronics goods to cosmetics, reported IAS net income fell 40 percent from the previous year to 511 million forints ($2.9 million).
